title: Double-Booking Detector
description: Interval shape on object input — sort depositions by start time, then a single scan comparing each event's start against the furthest end seen so far to surface scheduling conflicts.

conversation.intro: How an interview about a scheduling-conflict check would actually play out. Calendar integrity is bread-and-butter legal-tech work — a double-booked attorney is a missed deposition — so the interviewer will push hard on the overlap predicate and the touching-boundary case. Each section has two parts: what you'd actually say out loud, and why that move matters. Tap a section to expand.

sections.title: 1. Restate & clarify
sections.prompt: Interval problems live or die on the predicate — pin it down before you code.
sections.say:
"Let me restate: `findConflicts(events)` — I'm given one attorney's depositions, each `{ caseId, start, end }`, and I return every pair of caseIds whose time ranges overlap, because the attorney can't be in two rooms at once."

Then the clarifiers:
• Time format — zero-padded `'HH:MM'` 24-hour strings, `Date` objects, or minutes-since-midnight? Padded 24-hour strings compare correctly with a plain `<`, which saves me a parse step entirely. Unpadded `'9:00'` would break that, so I'd confirm the padding.
• Does everything fall on one day, or can a deposition run past midnight? Same-day is the sane assumption; multi-day means I need full timestamps, not clock strings.
• The boundary: one ends at 11:00 and the next starts at exactly 11:00 — conflict or not? Almost always NOT; back-to-back is legal. That single answer decides `<` versus `<=`.
• Output shape — every overlapping PAIR, or just the set of double-booked caseIds? Pairs are more useful (you can render 'A-101 collides with B-205'), and that's what the prompt asks for.
• Is the input already sorted? If it came out of a calendar query with `ORDER BY start` I can skip the sort and drop to O(n).
• Am I allowed to mutate the caller's array? `.sort()` does, so I'd clone with `[...events]` unless told otherwise.
sections.why: The boundary question is the whole problem in miniature: `<` versus `<=` is a one-character difference that turns every back-to-back appointment into a false conflict, and a scheduling tool that cries wolf gets switched off within a week. Asking about the time FORMAT is what earns you the right to write `curr.start < last.end` on raw strings instead of parsing — zero-padded `'HH:MM'` is fixed-width big-endian, so lexicographic order IS chronological order, exactly like ISO dates. Saying that out loud separates 'string comparison happens to work' from 'I know precisely why string comparison works here, and when it stops working.'

sections.title: 2. Brute force first (out loud)
sections.prompt: Say the O(n²) version, then say exactly what sorting buys you.
sections.say:
"The brute force is all-pairs: two nested loops over every (i, j) with i < j, and for each pair the general two-interval overlap test — `a.start < b.end && b.start < a.end`. That's O(n²) comparisons, but it's correct, it needs no preprocessing, and it takes thirty seconds to write. For one attorney's day n is maybe eight events; I'd honestly ship it.

What sorting buys me is the right to STOP comparing. Once events are ordered by start, the earlier one satisfies `a.start <= b.start`, and since `b.start < b.end`, the first clause `a.start < b.end` is true by construction — the sort proved it for me. So the symmetric two-sided test collapses to the one-sided `b.start < a.end`, which in the loop reads `curr.start < last.end`. Half the predicate disappears because the sort discharged it, and that's what takes me from O(n²) to one sort plus one linear sweep."
sections.why: Being able to write the general two-interval predicate `a.start < b.end && b.start < a.end` from memory is worth points on its own — plenty of candidates fumble the symmetric form. Then the optimization story tells itself: sorting DISCHARGES one half of the conjunction, so the sweep only has to check the other half. That is the actual reason the linear sweep is correct, and 'sorting lets me drop a clause' is a far stronger claim than 'sorting makes it faster'. Volunteering that you'd ship the O(n²) version at n=8 is a maturity signal too — you're optimizing because you were asked, not by reflex.

sections.title: 3. Spot the pattern — sort, then sweep against the FURTHEST end
sections.prompt: Which earlier event do you compare against, and why isn't it i-1?
sections.why: This is the section that decides the interview. 'Sort, then compare adjacent pairs' is the shape people half-remember from merge-intervals, and it silently produces wrong answers on NESTED intervals — a long deposition that swallows several short ones. Having the concrete A/B/C counterexample loaded means you can demonstrate the bug in ten seconds instead of asserting it. And stating the invariant explicitly — `last.end` is the running maximum — is what licenses the claim that a single comparison per event suffices. Without the invariant you're just hoping the sweep is correct; with it, the correctness argument is two lines.

sections.title: 4. Trace through examples
sections.prompt: Walk three inputs before committing to the loop.
sections.intro: "Let me run three inputs — the prompt's own calendar, the nested case that kills the i-1 version, and an unsorted pair that touches at a boundary." These are the same three inputs the Walkthrough tab steps through, so the two tabs tell one story.

examples.note: The L3 prompt's calendar. Two real collisions; the 11:00 handoff between B-205 and C-309 is clean because the test is strict.
The nested case — one all-day deposition swallowing two short ones. This is the example that proves `last` must track the furthest end, not index i-1.
examples.trace:
sorted by start = A-101@09:00 → B-205@10:00 → C-309@11:00
last = A-101 (ends 13:00)
i=1 curr=B-205: '10:00' < '13:00' → CONFLICT [A-101, B-205]; '10:30' > '13:00' false → last STAYS A-101
i=2 curr=C-309: '11:00' < '13:00' → CONFLICT [A-101, C-309]; '11:30' > '13:00' false → last STAYS A-101
return [["A-101","B-205"],["A-101","C-309"]]

(with a bare i-1 comparison, step i=2 would ask '11:00' < '10:30' → false and MISS the collision entirely)

examples.note: Two jobs at once: the input arrives out of order, so the sort prep step earns its keep, and the pair touches exactly at 11:00, so the strict `<` reports nothing.
examples.trace:
sorted by start = W-800@09:00 → X-900@11:00   (input order was reversed)
last = W-800 (ends 11:00)
i=1 curr=X-900: '11:00' < '11:00' → false → no conflict (back-to-back is legal); '12:00' > '11:00' → last = X-900
return []

sections.why: The nested example is the one to narrate out loud — it's the difference between an implementation that passes the happy path and one that's actually correct, and an interviewer who knows the problem is waiting to see whether you find it. The third example does double duty on purpose: it proves the clone-and-sort prep step isn't ceremony (without it the very first comparison is against the wrong event) AND it pins the `<` boundary. Reusing the boundary case as the degenerate case keeps the trace short without wasting an example slot.

sections.title: 5. Edge cases & failure modes
sections.prompt: What would trip up a careless implementation?
sections.say:
"Edges I'd walk through before calling it done:"

• Empty array — `sorted[0]` is `undefined`, but the loop guard `i = 1 < 0` is false immediately, so `last` is never dereferenced and we return `[]`. It works, but only by luck of the loop bound; I'd say that out loud so nobody thinks I missed it.
• Single deposition — same thing, no pairs, `[]`. ✓
• Exactly-touching pair (11:00 end, 11:00 start) → NOT a conflict under strict `<`. This is the test I'd write first.
• One-minute overlap (11:00 end, 10:59 start) → IS a conflict. The pair of tests above and below the boundary is what proves the predicate.
• Nested intervals — the running-max `last` handles them; a bare `i-1` scan does not.
• Identical start times — the comparator returns 0, and `Array.prototype.sort` has been stable since ES2019, so equal-start events keep input order. Both orderings still detect the conflict, but the PAIR ordering in the output would flip, so a test that asserts on exact pair order is fragile.
• Zero-length deposition (start === end) — `curr.start < last.end` still behaves; a zero-length event can be flagged against a container but never contains anything itself.
• Unpadded times like `'9:00'` — lexicographic comparison breaks (`'9:00' > '10:00'` is true as a string). Normalize to `'09:00'` on the way in, or parse to minutes.
• Events crossing midnight (`22:00`–`02:00`) — clock strings can't express this at all; end < start silently makes the event look empty. This needs real timestamps, and I'd flag it as out of scope rather than pretend the string version handles it.
• Reported pairs are only ADJACENT-in-the-sweep pairs. Three mutually overlapping depositions report as two pairs, not three. If the spec wants every colliding pair, that's a different algorithm (and O(output) can be quadratic).
sections.why: The last bullet is the honest one, and honesty scores here: this canonical reports a pair per conflicting event, not the full pairwise closure, and a careless candidate will claim 'it finds all conflicts' without noticing the difference. Naming the limit — and naming that full pairwise output can be quadratic no matter how clever you are, because the OUTPUT is quadratic — shows you understand the difference between an algorithm's cost and its contract. The midnight-crossing case is the domain call-out: clock strings are a modelling choice, and knowing where a modelling choice breaks is more valuable than knowing another sorting trick.

sections.title: 6. Complexity & wrap-up
sections.prompt: Defend the bounds, then generalize the template.
sections.why: Saying 'the sort is the entire cost' and then immediately giving the condition under which it disappears (pre-sorted input → O(n)) is a tighter complexity answer than the bound alone — it shows you know which term you'd attack. The four-way template table is the transfer move: the rusty engineer's real problem is that merge-intervals, meeting-rooms and activity-selection feel like three unrelated problems, and naming them as one skeleton with different carried state is exactly the handle that makes them recallable together. Ending on the Postgres exclusion constraint is the production-engineer note: an interviewer building a scheduling product will recognize instantly that you've shipped one.

walkthrough.intro: Step through the sort-then-sweep conflict scan. The state panel shows the `sorted` calendar, the current `curr`, the `last` pointer (the event with the FURTHEST end seen so far — not simply i-1), and the growing `conflicts` list. Watch the second example especially: a long deposition stays as `last` across several iterations, which is exactly the case a bare `sorted[i-1]` comparison would miss.

reference.approach: Sort by start, scan against furthest end
notes: Sort by start time first — overlap logic only holds once events are in chronological order.
Track the event with the furthest end seen so far, not just the immediately previous one: a long early deposition can overlap several later ones, which a bare `i-1` comparison would miss.
The overlap test is strict — `curr.start < last.end`. Touching boundaries (one ends exactly when the next starts) are NOT a conflict.

questions.q: Why sort the events by start time before scanning for conflicts?
options: Overlap detection compares each event to earlier ones — 'earlier' only means something on a chronologically ordered list
JavaScript requires arrays to be sorted before a for loop
Sorting converts the time strings into Date objects
questions.explain: Conflict detection is about whether an event starts before an earlier one ends. 'Earlier' is only well-defined once the events are sorted by start time.

questions.q: Why compare each event against the event with the FURTHEST end seen so far, rather than just the immediately previous event?
options: It makes the scan run faster
A long early deposition can overlap several later ones; comparing only to the immediately previous event would miss those conflicts
JavaScript cannot compare two array elements directly
Sorting by start guarantees the previous element is always the closest in time
questions.explain: Once sorted by start, the previous element isn't necessarily the one that ends latest. A 9:00–13:00 event overlaps everything starting before 13:00 — you must compare against the furthest-reaching end, not just index i-1.

questions.q: Given `curr` starts after `prev`, what condition means they overlap?
questions.explain: If the later event starts before the earlier one has ended (`curr.start < prev.end`), the two intervals overlap in time.

questions.q: One deposition ends at 11:00 and the next starts at exactly 11:00. Using `curr.start < last.end`, is that a conflict?
options: Yes — they touch, so they collide
No — the test is strict `<`, so a shared boundary is not an overlap
Yes — adjacent events in the sorted array always conflict
Only if the two share the same caseId
questions.explain: `'11:00' < '11:00'` is false, so back-to-back events that merely touch are not flagged. This matches reality: you can finish one deposition and start the next at the same minute.

exercises.prompt: Sort the events by start ascending, grab the first as `last`, and write the overlap test for the next event.

blanks.hint: array method that orders in place
strict comparison — touching boundaries don't conflict

exercises.prompt: Record a conflicting pair, then advance `last` only when the current event reaches further.

blanks.hint: the event that now ends latest

L3.prompt: Given an array of {caseId, start, end} depositions for one attorney, return an array of [caseId, caseId] pairs that overlap in time (the attorney can't be in two places at once).
hints: Sort by start time first, then walk the list once.
Keep a reference to the event with the furthest end so far; compare each new event's start against it.
Overlap is strict: `curr.start < last.end`. Advance `last` when `curr.end > last.end`.
